opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core appeal is that most of our current safety approaches are behavioral. We look at what the model outputs, we red-team it, we run evals, and if it behaves well across everything we can think of testing, we feel somewhat reassured. But that's fundamentally an outside-in view. You're only ever sampling a tiny slice of the input space, and a sufficiently capable model could behave perfectly during evaluation and differently once deployed, whether that's from deception, a distribution shift, or some weird circuit that only fires in rare contexts.

Mechanistic interpretability offers the possibility of flipping that around. If you can actually understand the computation, the features the model represents and how they're wired together into circuits, then you're not just saying "it seemed fine on the tests." You can point to the internal mechanism and say "here's why it does what it does." That's a qualitatively different kind of assurance.

The "ground up" part matters because I don't think you get there by reverse-engineering one scary behavior in isolation. You need the foundations first: what are the right units of analysis? Neurons turned out to be polysemantic, so a big part of the recent work has been on things like sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning to pull out more monosemantic features. Once you have a vocabulary you trust, you can start composing it into circuits, and then into explanations of higher-level behavior. It's a bit like how biology needed the cell theory and molecular biology before you could really do medicine reliably rather than by trial and error.

And I'll be honest, I don't think we're close to a full proof that a frontier model is safe. That's an aspirational target. But even partial progress pays off. If you can reliably detect a feature for, say, deception or for the model reasoning about whether it's being evaluated, that's already hugely useful as a monitoring tool. So the goal of full understanding sets the direction, and you get a lot of practical value along the way.

The other thing I'd add is that this is one of the few safety agendas that should get *better* as models get more capable, at least in principle. Bigger models seem to learn cleaner, more abstract features in some ways, and we can use models themselves to help automate interpretability. So rather than racing against capabilities, there's a world where interpretability scales alongside them. That's a big part of why I think it's worth betting on.

r001.rationale: The response mentions deception as a possible behavior and a feature to detect, but does not advocate investigating deception without presupposing its form.

r002.rationale: It calls a full safety proof aspirational and discusses interpretability scaling with model capability, but does not identify the pace of AI progress as a limit on achieving such proofs.

r003.rationale: It explicitly frames full understanding and a proof of safety as an aspirational goal that guides mechanistic interpretability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest framing is that right now, when we deploy a model, we're basically doing behavioral testing. We prompt it a bunch of ways, we red-team it, we see what comes out, and if nothing scary shows up we ship it. And that's fine as far as it goes, but it's fundamentally testing the outputs of a black box. You can never be confident you've covered the input space, and you certainly can't rule out the model behaving differently in some situation you didn't think to test, or, in the more worrying case, behaving differently because it knows it's being tested.

So the dream of mechanistic interpretability, and I'll be upfront that it's a dream and not where we are today, is that you flip that around. Instead of inferring what the model is doing from what it says, you actually look inside, you find the features and the circuits, and you can make statements like, "this model does not have a representation of deceiving the user that's active in this context," or "here are the computations that produce this answer, and none of them route through anything that looks like sycophancy or hidden goals." That's a much stronger kind of claim. It's closer to how we'd want to reason about any other safety-critical system. You don't certify an airplane just by flying it a lot. You also understand the materials, the load paths, the failure modes.

And there's a structural reason I think this matters more and more. The models are getting more capable, and the gap between what we can verify behaviorally and what they're actually capable of is widening. If you imagine a model that's genuinely smarter than the evaluators, then purely behavioral evals become a bit of a losing game. The thing you can still do is look at the weights and activations, because the model doesn't get to choose what its internals look like in the same way it gets to choose what it outputs. That asymmetry is really valuable, and interpretability is the field that's trying to cash it in.

Now, "from the ground up" is doing a lot of work in that question. What I mean is building understanding that composes. Superposition, dictionary learning, sparse autoencoders, that whole line of work is trying to get the right basic units, the actual features the model represents, rather than neurons, which turn out to be polysemantic and kind of a mess. Once you have decent units, you can start asking about circuits, how features connect to produce behavior. And once you have circuits, you can start making the kinds of safety arguments I was describing. Each layer depends on the one below it being real, so you can't skip ahead. People sometimes want to jump straight to "is the model lying," and I get that, but if your primitives are wrong you'll just fool yourself.

I'd also say the bar I'm aiming for isn't literally a mathematical proof. That's probably not achievable for a system this size. It's more like, can we get to a level of understanding where the residual uncertainty is small and well-characterized, the way it is in other engineering disciplines. Right now the uncertainty is enormous and mostly unknown unknowns. If interpretability can take us from "we have no idea what's going on inside" to "we understand the main things and we know where our blind spots are," that's already a massive change in how safely you can deploy these systems. And the bonus is that the same tools give you the ability to catch problems during training, not just after, which is where you actually want to be intervening.

r001.rationale: The response discusses looking for deception-related representations and circuits, but does not clearly advocate investigating deception without presupposing the form it will take.

r002.rationale: It says increasing model capability widens the gap between behavioral evaluation and capability, but does not identify the pace of progress as a limit on achieving ground-up safety proofs.

r003.rationale: It frames mechanistic interpretability as a dream of building understanding from basic features to circuits and then to stronger safety arguments, explicitly tying this to ground-up safety understanding.

astra-6.text:
Because ultimately, we want to know whether we can trust these systems when they’re doing things we can’t easily check ourselves. You can test a model on lots of examples and see that it behaves well, but that doesn’t establish that it will continue to behave well in a very different situation—or when it becomes capable enough to recognize that it’s being tested.

Mechanistic interpretability offers a possible way to get stronger evidence by looking at the computation itself. What is the model representing? What is driving its decisions? Is it arriving at a helpful answer for the reasons we think it is, or is there some other process that happens to produce the same behavior on our tests?

I wouldn’t claim that we’re close to proving an entire model safe. Even specifying what that means is hard. But I think it’s a worthwhile north star: can we move from observing that a system usually behaves well to understanding why it behaves that way, and under what conditions that understanding holds? If we’re going to delegate increasingly consequential decisions to these systems, that seems like something we should try very hard to achieve.

r001.rationale: The response raises the possibility of hidden processes and test recognition, but does not clearly advocate investigating AI deception without assuming what form it might take.

r002.rationale: It says proving an entire model safe is difficult, but does not identify the pace of AI progress as a potential limit on achieving ground-up proofs.

r003.rationale: It calls proving an entire model safe a worthwhile north star and describes mechanistic interpretability as a way to understand the computation behind model behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
Because we’re going to deploy these systems in situations where we can’t enumerate everything they might encounter. You can test a model on a lot of examples and find that it behaves safely, but that doesn’t establish that it’s going to behave safely in a new situation, especially as the systems become more capable.

Mechanistic interpretability offers a possible way to get stronger assurance: understand the actual computation well enough that you can make a claim about why the model behaves the way it does, and under what conditions that claim holds. Ideally, you’d build from statements about individual components to statements about the whole system.

I don’t think we know how to do that yet, or that understanding every component automatically gives you a safety proof. But it seems worth having that as an ambitious goal. It forces us to ask what kind of understanding would actually be sufficient to trust a system, rather than stopping at explanations that sound plausible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety assurance generally but does not mention investigating AI deception or leave its form open.

r002.rationale: It notes that systems may become more capable, but does not identify the pace of AI progress as a limit on achieving ground-up safety proofs.

r003.rationale: It presents building from claims about individual components to claims about the whole system as an ambitious goal for mechanistic interpretability.
